resumo.text: Este trabalho apresenta a concepção e implementação de um motor de formatação automática de documentos acadêmicos orientado por perfis institucionais declarativos. O problema investigado é a proliferação de lógica de formatação endurecida em código-fonte, que torna os sistemas de geração de documentos frágeis, de difícil manutenção e incapazes de suportar múltiplos perfis normativos sem alterações estruturais. A solução proposta separa de forma rigorosa as camadas de entrada, de perfil e de renderização, de modo que a adição de um novo perfil institucional não demande nenhuma alteração no motor de renderização. O trabalho descreve a arquitetura do sistema, os modelos de dados adotados, os mecanismos de layout para componentes de página única, o tratamento de blocos textuais com citações e formatação inline, e os mecanismos de indexação para listas de figuras, tabelas, quadros e gráficos. Os resultados demonstram que o motor é capaz de gerar documentos conformes com perfis distintos a partir de dados de entrada idênticos, validando a hipótese de separação entre dados, perfil e renderização.

entries.text: This work presents the design and implementation of an automatic formatting engine for academic documents driven by declarative institutional profiles. The investigated problem is the proliferation of hard-coded formatting logic in source code, which makes document generation systems fragile, difficult to maintain, and incapable of supporting multiple normative profiles without structural changes. The proposed solution rigorously separates the input, profile, and rendering layers so that adding a new institutional profile requires no changes to the rendering engine. Results demonstrate that the engine can generate documents compliant with distinct profiles from identical input data, validating the hypothesis of separation between data, profile, and rendering.

Este trabajo presenta la concepción e implementación de un motor de formateo automático de documentos académicos orientado por perfiles institucionales declarativos. El problema investigado es la proliferación de lógica de formateo codificada en el código fuente, que hace que los sistemas de generación de documentos sean frágiles, de difícil mantenimiento e incapaces de soportar múltiples perfiles normativos sin cambios estructurales. Los resultados demuestran que el motor puede generar documentos conformes con perfiles distintos a partir de datos de entrada idénticos.

APA

style regulates the structure and presentation of documents such as term papers, theses, and dissertations. However, existing formatting tools frequently embed normative rules directly in source code, resulting in coupled systems that are difficult to evolve.

Academic formatting standards establish visual and structural conventions for the presentation of scientific works. The
APA

publishes a set of style guidelines that regulate everything from page margins to the formatting of bibliographic references. Now in its 7th edition, the APA Publication Manual specifies pre-textual, textual, and post-textual elements for academic documents.

content.text: Internationally, other normative systems are widely adopted. The Chicago style, for example, offers two systems: author-date and bibliographic notes.
discuss how the choice of normative system affects the readability and standardization of documents produced in different fields of knowledge. Similarly,
argue that semantic modeling of document structure is a prerequisite for any normative-agnostic formatting engine.

Typographic composition systems such as LaTeX, Groff, and pandoc adopt declarative approaches to document formatting. In these systems, the author specifies the semantic structure of the document and the composition engine applies visual rules without the author having to manually control each presentation detail.

content.text: As shown in
, the proposed engine differs from existing systems by offering full support for APA style in an extensible manner, without coupling between normative rules and rendering code.

The principle of separation of concerns is widely documented in the software engineering literature. In the context of formatting systems, this means that presentation rules should not reside in the same component that processes semantic content.
According to
, applying this pattern in rendering engines reduces maintenance effort by up to 60% when new formatting profiles need to be introduced. This finding supports the central hypothesis of this work.

The internal representation of structured documents is a classic problem in computer science. Tree-based models — such as the
DOM
and the
XML

data model — are widely used for their ability to represent recursive content hierarchies. The model adopted in this work extends this concept to include profile rules as metadata associated with each node of the document tree.

Pre-textual components — such as the cover page, title page, and approval sheet — have a single-page structure with vertically positioned groups. The engine represents them as a set of content groups with space distribution rules between them.

This representation allows the profile to declare spacing weights between groups without knowing the actual height of the content, which is only known during rendering. The engine distributes the remaining space proportionally to the weights declared in the profile.

The strategy of anchoring the last group to the end of the safe page area is used to position city and year data at the bottom of the cover and title pages, as required by academic formatting standards.

This work adopts an applied research approach with incremental development. The methodology combines literature review, architectural design, and empirical validation through documented test cases. This work demonstrated that it is possible to build an academic document formatting engine completely driven by declarative profiles, without any conditional profile logic in the rendering code. The proposed architecture meets the fundamental principle established at the beginning of the research: any decision that may vary across profiles must reside in the profile, not in the code.

blocks.text: This questionnaire was administered to five specialists in APA style with the objective of evaluating the visual conformity of documents generated by the proposed engine in relation to the normative standard. Evaluators received pairs of documents — one generated by the engine and one formatted manually — without identification of origin, to minimize confirmation bias.
Question 1: Are the document margins in conformity with APA 7th edition (1 inch / 2.54 cm on all sides)?
Question 2: Is the line spacing in the body text double-spaced throughout, as prescribed?
Question 3: Are block quotations (40 words or more) indented 0.5 in. / 1.27 cm from the left margin with double spacing?
Question 4: Are Level 1 headings centered, bold, with title case, and without section numbering?
Question 5: Are references sorted alphabetically by first author surname, with a hanging indent of 1.27 cm and double spacing throughout?

items.title: APA 7th Edition — Summary of Required Elements

blocks.text: The APA Publication Manual (7th ed.) establishes the following as required pre-textual elements for student papers: title page and abstract. For professional manuscripts, a running head is also required. The remaining elements — table of contents, lists of figures and tables, and lists of abbreviations — are optional and institution-specific.

The body of an APA paper is organized by headings up to five levels. The post-textual elements include, as required, the references list. Optional elements include appendices, footnotes, and tables or figures placed at the end of the manuscript.

definitions: American Psychological Association. Organization responsible for the APA Publication Manual, the style guide widely adopted in psychology and related disciplines.
A direct quotation of 40 words or more, formatted as an indented block without quotation marks, according to APA style.
A structural element of a document with rules declared in the profile. May be a single-page component (such as the cover) or a flow-textual component (such as the abstract).
A declarative set of rules governing the formatting of a document type at a specific institution. The profile determines styles, component order, text templates, and layout behavior.
An indentation style in which the first line of a paragraph is flush with the margin and subsequent lines are indented. Required by APA style for reference list entries.
The process of transforming the content model and profile into formatted output (e.g., a DOCX file). The rendering engine contains no conditional profile logic.
